text: Why is a woman who's had many partners judged for it as someone who sleeps around, while a man who had many partners is praised for it as a stud? There are many reasons, because this is a complex topic. However, this creator is going to use flawed logic and research to explain why this bigoted view is apparently logical. It's a shame, because this creator has some good takes, but this is exactly why I caution my viewers against blindly following logical creators. A lot of so-called logical and factual creators tend to have inherent biases, and that's exactly what this creator is about to showcase. My videos haven't been challenged by anyone, at least relatively big, in quite a while. Some of you tagged me under a reaction by a creator called GU to a pretty old video of mine. In that video, I talk about a double standard, why a woman with many partners can be judged for sleeping around, while a man with many partners can be praised as a stud. Honestly, this is far from the worst response I've received. GU makes some interesting points and even praised me in the beginning. I appreciate that, but that still doesn't save you from my teardown. The response is more than 5 minutes long, so I won't play every clip. I'll explain what GU said and then answer it. Watch the full video if you want the complete context. First, let's go through my actual argument. I started by saying, people tend to respect outcomes that require effort, struggle, and difficulty, and they tend to value them much higher than outcomes that come easily. Then I argued that, in general, sleeping with someone is easier for women than for men. So if getting sexual partners is seen as harder for men, having many partners can be seen as more of an achievement for men. And my actual conclusion was, and that's one of the reasons why the same outcome, having many partners, can be perceived differently depending on who achieves it. One of the reasons. Keep that in mind. But GU introduces my video by saying I'm going to explain why this bigoted view is apparently logical. GU, if you're going to debunk someone, you should be more careful with your words. Explaining the thinking behind something is not the same as saying that thinking is correct. Imagine a friend gets cheated on and says, I'll never trust anyone again. You can understand the logic behind that reaction. He was hurt and he doesn't want it to happen again. But that doesn't mean his conclusion is logical or fair. Same here. Explaining why people might judge men and women differently does not mean saying they should. I explicitly said the purpose of this video is not to say what is right and what is wrong. The purpose is to explain why this perception exists in our society in the first place. You can challenge whether my explanation works, but don't turn it into an opinion I didn't express. Now, your first objection. I gave an example of two millionaires with the same fortune. One inherited it, the other started from zero, built a business and earned it. My point was that people could respect the second person more because of how they got there. You responded that supposedly self-made millionaires often had fortunate backgrounds and people actually admire the illusion of hard work. But there's no illusion in my example. I specifically ask you to imagine one person who genuinely started from zero and another who inherited the money. Saying some real millionaires didn't actually start from zero does not answer that comparison. You're changing the example instead of challenging it. You then added, if hard work led to success, then the donkey would own the farm. But I never said hard work guarantees success. Both millionaires already have the same fortune. The question is whether people respect them differently because of how they got it. The donkey has nothing to do with that. Next, the research. I described an experiment where strangers approached people on a campus and asked whether they would go to bed with them. Around 75% of men agreed, while no women agreed. I then claimed that later similar studies and follow-ups were done and the overall pattern stayed surprisingly or not surprisingly consistent. You responded that women's refusal reflects safety concerns, not ease. But those are not opposites. Safety concerns can explain why women refuse. And if fewer women agree, finding someone who agrees becomes harder for men. You've offered a possible reason for the difference. You haven't shown that the difference isn't there. Then, responding to my dating app example, you said more attention isn't more quality. But more offers and better offers are different things. I was comparing access to willing partners, not saying every offer is desirable. Some offers being unwanted does not show that men and women have equal access. That objection answers a different question. Next, you said attractive or privileged men can get sex easily and still be celebrated. So, if easy outcomes get mocked, my argument should predict that those men get mocked too. But you are treating a general tendency as if it must apply equally to every man, including those with obvious advantages. There's a difference between something being seen as difficult for men generally and being easier for attractive or privileged men, like Marlon in your example. Those advantages do not automatically erase the wider perception. Think of the football example. Women succeeding in elite men's football could receive enormous praise even if they had obvious advantages. Exceptional natural talent, access to the best coaches, or both. Those advantages would not automatically erase how difficult people generally see that achievement as being for women. And my millionaire example did not mean nobody could admire the person who inherited the money. It meant the person who earned it could receive more respect for the achievement. You also said mocking a rich kid is not the same as shaming a woman. I never said it was. I said difficulty is one of the reasons the same outcome is perceived differently. How harsh the judgment gets is a separate question. Finally, you offer your own explanation for the double standard, pointing to paternity and inheritance. Men wanting to know that the children inheriting their property were actually theirs. Fair enough. But giving another explanation does not automatically disprove mine. I explicitly said one of the reasons. I didn't say the one and only reason. So you don't have to agree with my premise. But if you want to challenge my argument, show where it goes wrong. Changing my example, answering a different question, or treating one reason as if I claimed it explained everything does not do that. Thanks for the response, Gio.
